msg: Paper 75 deals with the default of Adam and Eve. Adam labored for more than a hundred years, yet the world outside the Garden had changed very little. The divine plan for uplifting humankind seemed far too slow. At that point Serapatatia, a Nodite leader, proposed a shortcut: that Eve unite with a superior Nodite leader so as to raise up a powerful race more quickly. Eve was won over by the proposal. Today's passage precisely defines the moral character of this event.

The passage says that even though this project of modifying the divine plan had been conceived and executed with entire sincerity and with only the highest motives concerning the welfare of the world, it constituted evil. There are two reasons: because it represented the wrong way to achieve righteous ends, and because it departed from the right way, the divine plan. Paper 75 repeatedly emphasizes that Serapatatia was honest and sincere in all that he proposed. Eve, too, had no intention whatsoever of harming Adam's mission. That something begun in good faith should end in so great a tragedy gives us a deep warning.

This teaching sets forth a very important moral principle. Good intentions alone are not enough. Even when the end is right, if the means are wrong, the act becomes evil. We often think that if the motive is good, everything is forgiven. Motives certainly matter, and God looks upon our hearts. But good motives do not justify wrong methods. Eve's mistake did not come from an evil heart but from impatience and from placing her own judgment ahead of the divine plan.

This event strangely resembles Caligastia's rebellion. Lucifer and Caligastia also claimed that they knew a better way. They regarded the divine plan as too slow and confining. Eve's case differs in that there was no intent to rebel, yet it is the same in that the appointed path was abandoned because the plan seemed slow. Paper 75 also relates that after Caligastia failed to tempt Adam directly, he cunningly approached Eve. Evil does not always come in an open form; sometimes it arrives clothed in the noblest of purposes.

Such temptations often come in our lives as well. When we want to accomplish something good but the honest path seems too slow, we are tempted to justify a small lie or a shortcut. We think that for the sake of our family, for the sake of the community, for the sake of God's work, bending the rules a little might be all right. But wrong means end up undermining even the good end itself. In the case of Adam and Eve, too, the shortcut brought down the whole plan.

So we must examine not only our ends but also our ways. The Father's will lies not only in the outcome but also in the process that leads to it. The honest path that seems slow is in fact the surest one. When impatience arises, we must pause and ask whether this method is a path God would be pleased with. The leading of the Thought Adjuster usually takes us not along shortcuts but along the right way. A small fruit gathered on the right path lasts far longer than a great success gained on a wrong one.
d148.pr: Recall a time you were tempted to use a shortcut to reach a good end, and write down what the right way would be, even if slower.

msg: The final section of Paper 75 corrects the age-old doctrine of the so-called fall of man. Adam and Eve fell from the high estate of a Material Son to the lowly status of mortal man, but that was not the fall of man. On the contrary, the human race was uplifted by Adam's contribution. And as the revelator closes this tragic story, he leaves us today's passage, a profound reflection on why a universe in which failure and disagreement are possible is, in fact, glorious.

The passage begins with a supposition. If this were a mechanistic universe, if the First Great Source and Center were only a force and not also a personality, if all creation were a vast aggregation of physical matter dominated by precise laws, then perfection might obtain, with no disagreement and no friction. But in our evolving universe of relative perfection and imperfection, the revelators say, we rejoice that disagreement and misunderstanding are possible, for thereby is evidenced the fact and the act of personality in the universe. The revelators value a universe of imperfect but living personalities above the perfect but lifeless order of a machine.

The passage then draws its conclusion. If our creation is an existence dominated by personality, then can you be assured of the possibilities of personality survival, advancement, and achievement; we can be confident of personality growth, experience, and adventure. And it exclaims, “⟦Q 75:8.7⟧What a glorious universe, in that it is personal and progressive, not merely mechanical or even passively perfect!⟦/Q⟧” This cry of wonder is all the more moving for bursting forth at the very place where the failure of Adam and Eve has just been told.

This teaching changes the way we see suffering and failure. We often ask why God made a world in which mistakes and evil are possible. The revelator's answer is this: a being who cannot err cannot choose, and a being who cannot choose cannot love. A machine runs without error, but it does not grow. A personality can rise because it can fall, and can truly choose what is right because it can do wrong. Perfection is not a state given from the beginning but a goal attained through experience.

The Universal Father made us not as perfectly functioning machines but as free sons and daughters. That freedom carries risk, but because of that risk our love, loyalty, and growth are real. So it was with Adam and Eve. They failed, but they repented, rose again, and served to the end in the second garden. Their failure was not an end but a stage in their personal growth. Paper 76 tells us that they at last resumed the path of ascension.

So we need not despair before our own mistakes or the conflicts between people. Disagreement and misunderstanding are painful, but they are evidence that we are living personalities. If you had friction with someone today, you can make it an occasion for understanding and growth. If you have fallen, simply rise again. Let us give thanks from the depths of our hearts today for a universe that calls us to learn, grow, and adventure through our mistakes; what a glorious universe it is. We are not finished machines but growing sons and daughters.
d149.pr: Recall one mistake or conflict you experienced today, and with gratitude write down how it might help you grow.

msg: Paper 76 deals with the life that Adam and Eve, having left the first garden, spent in the second garden in Mesopotamia, and with their deaths. They repented and devoted the rest of their lives to teaching their children and neighbors. After Adam's death, Urantia was again left to the evolutionary races. The plight of this planet, beset by both rebellion and default, seems truly unfortunate. But at exactly this point, today's passage tells of an astonishing reversal: misfortune has not been the sole lot of Urantia.

According to the passage, this planet has also been the most fortunate in the local universe of Nebadon. The blunders of their ancestors and the mistakes of their early world rulers so plunged the planet into a hopeless state of confusion, all the more confounded by evil and sin, that this very background of darkness appealed to Michael of Nebadon; and if he therefore selected this world as the arena wherein to reveal the loving personality of the Father in heaven, then, the passage says, Urantians should count it all gain. A history that looks like a string of misfortunes to human eyes appeared to the eyes of heaven in an entirely different light.

The passage makes one thing clear. It is not that Urantia needed a Creator Son to set its tangled affairs in order. It is rather that the evil and sin on Urantia afforded the Creator Son a more striking background against which to reveal the matchless love, mercy, and patience of the Paradise Father. Just as stars shine brighter in a dark night sky, the darkness of this earth made Michael's life shine all the more gloriously. God's love was revealed most vividly in the deepest darkness.

This teaching profoundly changes the way we look at hardship. We sometimes feel it a misfortune to have been born into this world. We find ourselves asking why we must live on such a confused and painful planet. But the revelator tells us that this very planet is where the Creator Son lived in human flesh. Among the countless worlds of the universe, only this one became the stage for Michael's seventh bestowal. This is a glory that no suffering can erase. The manger of Bethlehem, the workshop of Nazareth, and the roads of Galilee are all on this small planet. That is why so many beings in the universe look upon this world with wonder.

The same principle applies to our personal lives. Our mistakes, wounds, and dark seasons are not good in themselves, but God can turn them into a background that reveals his love. Those who have fallen the deepest come to know grace most deeply, and those who have passed through the darkest places treasure the light the most. God does not desire our suffering, but he does not let even that suffering go to waste. A wound can become a place where grace abides.

So today we can give thanks that we are citizens of Urantia. We live on the earth where Jesus walked, in the world where he worked, taught, and loved. And we can believe that even the dark parts of our lives can become a background that reflects God's love. Rather than resenting misfortune, to look within it for the grace that shines all the brighter: this is the fitting attitude for those who live on the most fortunate planet.
d150.pr: Recall one dark season of your life, and look for the love and grace of God revealed within it, and give thanks.

d151.t: A Mind No Evil Spirit Can Possess
msg: Paper 77 introduces the midway creatures, who exist on a level between mortals and angels. The primary midwayers sprang from Caligastia's staff, and the secondary midwayers from the children of Adamson. But some of them joined the rebellion. The seventh section deals with these rebel midwayers and explains that part of the phenomenon the ancient world called demoniacal possession was in fact their activity. Today's passage reveals an important truth about that phenomenon. The revelator does not hide this dark subject but explains it honestly, while carefully drawing boundaries so as not to plunge us into fear.

The passage declares that on no world can evil spirits possess any mortal mind subsequent to the life of a Paradise bestowal Son. Before the days of Christ Michael on Urantia, before the universal coming of the Thought Adjusters and the pouring out of the Master's spirit upon all flesh, these rebel midwayers were actually able to influence the minds of certain inferior mortals and somewhat to control their actions. But after Michael's bestowal and Pentecost, the situation changed completely. The very next paragraph tells us that the entire group of rebel midwayers is now held in custody.

This teaching frees many people from fear. For ages people lived in dread that an evil spirit might at any moment enter their minds and control them. Even today some are gripped by such fear. But the Urantia Book says plainly that since Michael came to this earth, evil spirits cannot take possession of our minds. Our minds are a sanctuary indwelt by the Thought Adjuster, a place where the Spirit of Truth abides.

This does not mean that we face no temptation. We still struggle with our own selfishness, our animal nature, and our mistaken thoughts. But we ourselves are the protagonists of that struggle, and the power of decision is ours. The excuse that the devil made us do it no longer holds. Our choices are our responsibility. This is a weighty responsibility and at the same time a great dignity. Our minds are a matter between ourselves and God. So we must honestly acknowledge our wrongs and ask the Father for the strength to overcome them.

The passage also says that loyal midwayers function as contact guardians of the human minds of the Urantia reserve corps of destiny. In much the same way that the rebel midwayers once disturbed human minds, loyal midwayers now protect and assist them. The same ability, used for rebellion, does harm; used in loyalty, it becomes a blessing. This contrast shows that the worth of every ability is finally determined by the purpose to which it is devoted.

So today we can live by trust instead of fear. There is no need to shrink back in dread of the powers of darkness. Michael has already triumphed, and the Father's spirit dwells within us. What is ours to do is to choose each day to whom we will open the door of our minds. When we open our hearts toward truth, beauty, and goodness, our inner life becomes a peaceful sanctuary where we walk with God. Let not fear but love be the master of our hearts.
d151.pr: Name one vague fear, lay it down as you remember the Father's spirit within you, and offer a prayer for peace.

msg: After explaining in detail the origin, history, and present duties of the midway creatures, Paper 77 in its final section calls them the permanent citizens of Urantia. Seraphim come and go, but the midwayers remain on this planet. After Adam and Eve departed, they became skilled ministers bridging the gap between material and spiritual affairs. Today's passage gathers this whole story into one great picture, showing within what plan of the universe the service of the midwayers is set.

The passage says that the entire organization of high spirits, angelic hosts, and midway fellows is enthusiastically devoted to the furtherance of the Paradise plan for the progressive ascension and perfection attainment of evolutionary mortals. This plan, one of the supernal businesses of the universe, is the superb survival plan. It brings God down to man and then, by a sublime sort of partnership, carries man up to God and on to eternity of service and divinity of attainment. And it adds that this plan holds alike for mortal and midwayer.

This passage beautifully holds the two directions of salvation. The first direction comes down from above. God first comes to man: the Thought Adjuster indwells our minds, Michael came in human flesh, and the Spirit of Truth was poured out. The second direction goes up from below. Man, entering into partnership with the God who has thus drawn near, ascends step by step toward the Father. Our ascension is not a solitary climb but a journey walked together with God. Had God not come first, we could not even have found him.

Another moving fact is that countless beings are enthusiastically devoted to this plan. Even when we do not see it, angels, midwayers, and high spirits are helping our growth. They do not work from a sense of duty alone; the passage says they are enthusiastically devoted. For them, a single mortal seeking God and growing is both a joy and a mission. We are living within a vast fellowship of love.

It is also worth noting that the passage says this plan holds for midwayers too. The midwayers, too, will someday walk the path of ascension and reach Paradise. The beings who help us are fellows walking with us toward the same goal. In the universe, helpers and the helped are not divided forever; a brotherhood flows through it in which all help one another and grow together. This is the true face of the universe family. That higher and lower beings walk together toward the same goal shows how warm a place the universe is.

So today we can remember two things. One is that I am never alone. God came to me first, and countless unseen fellows are helping my journey. The other is that I too can become a worker in this plan. Every kindness and encouragement that helps a neighbor take one more step toward God is a share in the very work the angels and midwayers do. Today let us also join in this great enterprise of bringing God down to man and carrying man up to God.
d152.pr: Give thanks for the unseen beings who help you, and today offer a warm word of encouragement that helps a neighbor draw nearer to God.

msg: Paper 78 traces the path the violet race followed after the deaths of Adam and Eve. The second garden in Mesopotamia was the cradle of civilization for almost thirty thousand years. There the descendants of Adam preserved a center of culture and religion and spread their influence steadily into the surrounding world. Today's passage praises the heroism shown by the leaders of the second garden during this period. The revelator calls it one of the amazing and inspiring epics of Urantia's history.

According to the passage, these splendid souls never wholly lost sight of the purpose of the Adamic mission. They valiantly fought off the influences of the surrounding and inferior tribes, while they willingly sent forth their choicest sons and daughters in a steady stream as emissaries to the races of earth. The passage adds that this expansion was sometimes depleting to the home culture, but always these superior peoples would rehabilitate themselves. Here is the picture of a community that gives itself away and yet is filled again. They were not swept away by the lower influences of the world around them, yet neither did they turn their backs on that world. They managed both to guard and to share.

What touches the heart most in this passage is the phrase that they sent forth their choicest sons and daughters. It is not easy for a community to let go of the people it treasures most. Had they stayed, the homeland might have prospered more. But the leaders of the second garden put the mission of uplifting all humankind ahead of their own prosperity. The plan that Adam and Eve had failed to accomplish, their descendants carried forward little by little through the sacrifice of gladly giving up their own share.

This shows that Adam's default did not end everything. The divine plan had gone badly awry, but its spirit survived in loyal descendants. The children of parents who had failed remembered the mission and devoted themselves to it. As the whole of Paper 78 shows, the culture and bloodlines that spread from the second garden later became the leaven that awakened the civilizations of Europe, Asia, and Africa. Sacrificial sharing was never in vain. That the failure of the parents could not prevent the loyalty of the children gives us great hope.

This principle applies to our lives as well. Whether a family, a church, or a community, holding tightly to what is best may bring abundance for a while, but in the end it stagnates and spoils. On the other hand, a community that gives its best to the world, though it may look empty for a time, is filled again and gains greater life. We experience this truth when parents send their children out into the world, and when teachers send their disciples on to new missions. Life increases when it is shared.

Jesus too sent his disciples into all the world. He sent to the farthest places the very people he might have wished to keep closest. And through that sending, the gospel spread over all the earth. Today we too can ask ourselves: am I gladly sending forth the best I have, my time, my talents, and my love, for the sake of the world? When we give, remembering the mission as the heroes of the second garden did, our lives too will be restored and renewed. Giving is not loss but a door into greater life.
d153.pr: Today, gladly give for someone else's sake some of the time or talent you have been holding tightly to yourself.

msg: The last paragraph of Paper 78 sums up in a word the fate of the violet race and their homeland, Mesopotamia. The story that unfolded over tens of thousands of years after Adam was full of glory and decline, migration and mixture, flood and invasion. The Andites scattered in every direction, and the last remaining Sumerians were finally conquered by invaders from the north. Today's passage tells the ending of this long history, and at the same time reveals the deep meaning hidden within it.

The passage says that their ancient civilization finally fell due to the emigration of superior peoples and the immigration of their inferior neighbors. On the surface this is the record of a sad defeat. But the passage immediately adds that long before the barbarian cavalrymen conquered the valley, much of the Garden culture had spread to Asia, Africa, and Europe, there to produce the ferments which have resulted in the twentieth-century civilization of Urantia. The homeland fell, but its culture did not vanish; it seeped into the whole world. Even in a record of defeat, the revelator never lets go of hope.

The word ferment is deeply meaningful. Leaven hides in the flour, working unseen, and makes the whole dough rise. So it was with the culture left by Adam's descendants. They did not build an empire bearing their name, and their cities became ruins. But the knowledge, skills, and spiritual traditions they passed on blended into many peoples and became the foundation of the civilization we enjoy today. Papers 79 and 80 tell in detail how this leaven worked in the East and the West.

This truth changes our standard for measuring success and failure. We tend to measure success by visible achievements and lasting buildings. But from heaven's point of view, true influence may be what seeps in unseen. Even if a community crumbles, if the people and values it nurtured bear fruit throughout the world, that is not failure but another form of victory. A seed bears much fruit only when it falls into the ground and disappears. There is no need to lose heart by looking only at today's results. In God's time, our labors bear fruit in ways we never imagined.

Jesus too compared the kingdom of heaven to leaven. Like the leaven a woman hid in three measures of meal until the whole was leavened, the kingdom of heaven transforms the world quietly but surely. What he established was not a visible kingdom. He planted truth in the hearts of a few disciples, and that truth spread throughout the world through the scattered disciples. Scattering became spreading. This is often how God's work is done. As with a small seed and a bit of leaven, the growth of the kingdom of heaven is at first hardly noticed.

Each of our lives can become leaven too. What we accomplish may not stand out, and the community we belong to may one day disappear. But the love and truth we have given our neighbors by living sincerely go on working unseen in their lives. Passed on again to others, they make the world rise little by little. May I be good leaven wherever I go today. Leaven that works unseen changes the world most deeply.
d154.pr: Choose one small way to exert a quiet, good influence among the people you meet today, and put it into practice.

msg: Paper 79 deals with the history of the Andite expansion into the Orient, the story of their spread into Turkestan, India, and China. The sixth section explains how Chinese civilization began, summing up the reasons the yellow race achieved a great civilization under three heads: biologic, social, and spiritual. Biologically, they avoided admixture with inferior strains; socially, they early learned the value of peace among themselves. Today's passage deals with the third, the spiritual factor.

The passage says that during the age of Andite migrations the Chinese were among the more spiritual peoples of earth. Long adherence to the worship of the One Truth proclaimed by Singlangton kept them ahead of most of the other races. The passage then states a general principle: the stimulus of a progressive and advanced religion is often a decisive factor in cultural development. And it says that as India languished, so China forged ahead under the invigorating stimulus of a religion in which truth was enshrined as the supreme Deity. When religion is alive, a people moves forward; when religion hardens, the people comes to a standstill with it.

The phrase that truth was enshrined as the supreme Deity is very striking. Unlike many primitive religions that served ghosts or natural forces as objects of fear, the faith of the yellow race honored truth itself as the highest value. This was a religion in which reason and faith were in harmony. Those who worship truth hate falsehood, love learning, and face reality honestly. Such a spiritual attitude led naturally to advances in learning, technology, and social order.

This passage teaches an important lesson about the relation between religion and civilization. We often think of the advance of civilization only as a matter of economics and technology. But the Urantia Book tells us that a living religion can be the driving force of civilization. Conversely, when religion loses its vitality and only form remains, civilization stagnates along with it. Paper 79 relates that India's spiritual awakening was not sustained, and that China too, inclining later toward ancestor worship, slowed in its progress (see Paper 79). The vitality of religion is neither easily won nor automatically maintained. The love of truth, in the end, renews the whole of life.

Jesus said, “⟦Q 141:7.6⟧You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.⟦/Q⟧” He also said that he was the way, the truth, and the life. In the Urantia Book, truth is one of the divine attributes of the Father, and the Spirit of Truth leads us into all truth. A heart that loves truth is bound up with a heart that loves God. Singlangton's worship of the One Truth, imperfect as it was, was a sincere human response to this eternal reality.

Today we can ask whether our own faith is open toward truth. Has my religion stopped at fear and habit, or is it growing toward living truth? Those who serve truth as the highest value learn every day, live honestly, and remain humble before new insight. Such faith renews the individual and, beyond that, leads a society and a civilization forward. The honest life of one person who loves truth has a wider influence than we might think.
d155.pr: Today, speak honestly without small lies or exaggerations, practicing serving truth as the highest value.

msg: The last section of Paper 79 deals with the later Chinese civilization, and alongside the great achievements of the yellow race it honestly points out the factors that slowed their progress. One of these was ancestor veneration. The revelator weighs its strengths and weaknesses with balance. Its strength was that it placed great value on the family, giving rise to the remarkable stability and continuity of Chinese culture. Today's passage addresses its weakness and in doing so offers a profound insight into the nature of truth. Whether praising or criticizing a culture, the revelator always uses fair scales.

The passage says that the great weakness of ancestor veneration is that it promotes a backward-looking philosophy. However wise it may be to glean wisdom from the past, it is folly to regard the past as the exclusive source of truth. And then it defines truth: truth is relative and expanding; it lives always in the present, achieving new expression in each generation of men, even in each human life. It is a short sentence, yet wonderfully rich.

This teaching shows a balanced attitude toward tradition. The Urantia Book does not tell us to ignore the past. The wisdom of our ancestors is a precious heritage, and we can learn a great deal from it. But the moment we treat the past as the only storehouse of truth, we turn living truth into a fossil. Truth is not a relic kept in a museum; it is life breathing within us today. Yesterday's insight is today's starting point, not its destination. Honoring the past and being imprisoned by it are entirely different things.

This principle matters especially for religion. Many religious traditions tend to absolutize past revelation and so cannot receive new truth. When scriptures and doctrines harden, faith ceases to be a living experience and becomes the guarding of old records. The Urantia Book teaches that religion must always evolve and expand. The Spirit of Truth speaks afresh to each generation, and the Thought Adjuster reveals truth anew within each person. God is not only the God of yesterday but the God of today.

The passage says that truth achieves new expression in each human life. This is a wondrous dignity. Even the same truth, passing through my life, takes on a color all its own. The love Jesus taught is one, yet the ways of living that love blossom differently in countless lives. We are not beings who merely copy truth but creative personalities who express it anew. Each person's life becomes a new chapter of truth. That is why each of our lives holds a unique worth that no one else can replace.

So today we can hold together gratitude for the past and openness to the present. We should treasure the wisdom received from parents, teachers, and elders in faith, yet not stop there. We must listen for how truth comes to us freshly in today's experience, and we must express that truth anew through our own lives. Truth lives always in the present, and it is always calling us forward. The truth I meet today may be a handbreadth wider than yesterday's.
d156.pr: Reflect on one idea you have long held, and consider how today's experience might deepen it.

msg: Paper 80 tells the history of the Andite expansion into the Occident, the story of how the descendants of Adam spread into Europe, North Africa, and the Mediterranean islands. At that time Europe was widely populated by the Cro-Magnoid blue men. The third section introduces these blue men and the civilization they formed as they blended with the Adamites. Today's passage summarizes the character of early post-Adamic European civilization, frankly revealing both its achievements and the price it paid. The process by which two different streams meet and form a new civilization is a story of both hope and regret.

The passage says that the European civilization of this early post-Adamic period was a unique blend of the vigor and art of the blue men with the creative imagination of the Adamites. The blue men were a race of great vigor, but they greatly deteriorated the cultural and spiritual status of the Adamites. It was very difficult for the Adamites to impress their religion upon the Cro-Magnoids because of the tendency of so many to cheat and to debauch the maidens. As a result, for ten thousand years religion in Europe was at a low ebb as compared with the developments in India and Egypt.

This passage shows that the meeting of cultures always works in two directions. When different peoples meet, their strengths combine and a new power arises. The vigor of the blue men and the imagination of the Adamites came together to give birth to the distinctive vitality of European civilization. Yet at the same time, the weakness of one side can drag down the strength of the other. The lofty spiritual tradition of the Adamites could not take root in a morally lax environment. Blending can be a blessing or a loss. So when cultures meet, we need the wisdom to discern what to receive and what to preserve.

What deserves special attention here is the reason the spiritual tradition failed to be passed on. It was not a lack of intellectual ability but a matter of moral character. Where deceit and debauchery prevail, high religion can hardly grow. Religion is not transmitted by knowledge alone; it needs an honest and clean heart to receive it. As in Jesus' parable of the sower, even good seed bears no fruit on rocky ground or among thorns. Spiritual truth grows in moral soil.

This teaching applies directly to our own spiritual lives today. We long to learn much spiritual truth, yet we easily neglect everyday honesty, purity, and faithfulness. But when small lies and excesses pile up, the soil of the heart grows hard, and even the finest teaching cannot take root. On the other hand, truth sinks deep into the heart of one who lives honestly and with restraint, and it bears abundant fruit. Morality is the vessel of spirituality. If we wish to climb to spiritual heights, we must first set right the small honesties of daily life.

At the same time, this passage offers the hope that great civilizations are born when vigor and imagination come together. Within us, too, dwell both the vigor to live life fully and the creative imagination that dreams of higher things. When we build both upon an honest and clean character, our lives can grow in balance like a healthy civilization. Today let us tend the soil of our hearts with care, preparing it so that the seeds of heaven may grow well.
d157.pr: Find one small habit that hardens the soil of your heart, and keep away from it throughout this day.

msg: The seventh section of Paper 80 recounts the history of the Andites who entered the Mediterranean islands, especially Crete and Greece. This region, linking Mesopotamia and Egypt, became the Western center of trade, art, and culture. The astonishing genius of the Greeks was a heritage handed down from Adamson and his descendants. Yet in the midst of this story of a brilliant culture, today's passage quietly records a sorrowful fact: by about 6500 B.C. there had occurred a great decline in the spiritual heritage of the Andites.

The passage says that the descendants of Adam were widespreadly dispersed and had been virtually swallowed up in the older and more numerous human races. And this decadence of Andite civilization, together with the disappearance of their religious standards, left the spiritually impoverished races of the world in a deplorable condition. Art, trade, and culture were still flourishing, but the spiritual tradition that was the very soul of those civilizations was fading. Outward prosperity and inward poverty existed side by side. The flowers of culture were in bloom, but the roots that had brought them forth were slowly withering.

This record gives us an important warning. For a civilization to prosper materially and artistically is one thing; to be spiritually alive is another. The very time when the culture of the Aegean world was blossoming, the revelator records as an age of spiritual decline. Even with splendid temples and beautiful statues, a civilization without a faith that knows the living God is spiritually poor. However dazzling its outward appearance, a civilization that is hollow within cannot long endure.

We should also note the cause of this spiritual decline. As the descendants of Adam scattered and intermingled, they failed to keep their religious standards. Their bloodlines and culture spread widely, but the awareness of God and the tradition of worship at their core did not spread with them; it was diluted. This confirms once again the truth, taught in Paper 68, that civilization is not biologically inherited but is passed on only when it is consciously taught (see Paper 68). A spiritual heritage does not preserve itself. When one generation neglects its faith, the loss carries on for many generations.

Yet this dark record is not the end of the story. Heaven kept working for a spiritually impoverished world. After this decline Machiventa Melchizedek appeared and rekindled the flame of monotheism through the teachings of Salem (see Paper 93), and at last Michael himself came to this world. Whenever humanity has lost its spiritual heritage, God has come again with new revelation. An age of spiritual poverty is always also an age of longing for fresh revelation.

Today we can learn two things from this history. First, we must stay awake so as not to lose our spiritual center amid the prosperity of our personal lives, families, and communities. We should examine whether prayer and worship are being pushed aside by busy routines and abundance. Second, we must faithfully pass on to the next generation the spiritual heritage we have received. When we keep and share a living faith under the guidance of the Thought Adjuster, our age may be recorded not as one of spiritual decline but of spiritual renewal. That is how we can take up again the heritage that the descendants of Adam failed to keep.
d158.pr: Even if only for today, lovingly reclaim a time of prayer or worship that busy days have pushed aside.

msg: Today's passage changes the way we look at civilization. We usually treat civilization as a right that comes to us automatically at birth. We assume that electricity and running water, law and schools, hospitals and libraries are simply there, like the air. But The Urantia Book says that cultural society is no great and beneficent club of inherited privilege; rather, it is a guild of earth workers who toil to make a better world for their descendants. To join its ranks one must pay costly admission fees and keep strict disciplines. It adds that heavy penalties are visited on all dissenters and nonconformists. Civilization demands the devotion of those who uphold it, and the attitude that wants only its benefits without that devotion ends up weakening the whole community.

Paper 81 tells how long and arduous a road humanity traveled from hunter to herder, and then to farmer and city dweller. Every step, from mastering fire and taming animals to smelting metals and learning to write, bears the marks of earlier generations who set aside their own comfort and labored. Civilization is not a building that, once erected, stands forever; it is a living structure that can collapse unless each generation holds it up anew. That is why this paper emphasizes that the character of those who pass the torch to the next generation determines the destiny of civilization.

Here the phrase the nobility of those toilers resonates deeply. True nobility is determined not by lineage or wealth but by what one adds for the next generation. Those concerned only with securing their own share may enjoy the benefits of civilization, but they do not become its true members. On the other hand, the ordinary people who work faithfully in places no one notices, holding up the community, are the full members of this guild. The words that the guild confers few personal licenses or privileges except those of enhanced security against common dangers remind us that we have more to give than to receive. We often speak of rights first and duties later, but this passage reverses the order. To contribute first and enjoy afterward is the age-old rule of the guild of civilization.

This teaching also touches the spiritual life. Jesus came not to be served but to serve, and he taught that the greatest in the kingdom of God is the one who serves all. To take part in the guild of civilization is to practice brotherhood. The small labors we do today, one task handled honestly, one hour given for a neighbor, quietly accumulate to become stepping-stones for the next generation. And through each such choice that rises above selfishness, the Thought Adjuster nurtures our souls. That labor for society is inseparable from the growth of the soul is a truth The Urantia Book teaches again and again. The habit of service learned by ministering to our neighbors in this world carries over into the morontia worlds and the ascending journey beyond.

Today, consider how much of what you enjoy has come from the sacrifices of nameless generations before you. Then, with a grateful heart, resolve to become a worker who adds something for those who will come after. That is the way to pay gladly the admission fee of the exalted guild of civilization.
d159.pr: Choose one convenience you enjoyed today and give thanks as you recall the labor of past generations hidden behind it.

d160.t: No Stream Rises Above Its Source
msg: Paper 81 lists one after another the factors that sustain and advance civilization. Climate and natural resources, scientific knowledge and human resources, language and mechanical devices, education and leadership are all mentioned. Among them, today's passage speaks of the racial ideals: the ideals of one generation carve out the channels of destiny for immediate posterity. And it presents a simple yet solemn principle: no stream will rise any higher than its source. These words point to the deepest place among all the factors Paper 81 lists. However abundant the resources and technology, if the ideals that decide what they are used for are low, a civilization may instead be crushed under the weight of its own power.

No matter how hard water is pumped, it cannot in the end rise above the height of its source. The same is true of society. However elaborate its institutions and however strong its controls, a society cannot long advance beyond the height of the ideals its members hold. The passage says that the driving power of even the most material aspects of a cultural civilization is resident in the least material of society's achievements. Intelligence may control the mechanism of civilization, wisdom may direct it, but spiritual idealism is the energy which really uplifts and advances human culture from one level of attainment to another.

These words cast the responsibility of home, church, and school in a new light. The passage says that the homes, churches, and schools of one generation predetermine the character trend of the succeeding generation. The greatest legacy parents leave their children is not property but the ideals they have shown by their lives. A child raised by parents who teach honesty in words but compromise in deeds does not learn the height of honesty. On the other hand, parents who live simply but truly prepare a high source in their child's heart.

Looking back on history, there are many examples of materially rich civilizations that lost their ideals and declined. Conversely, small and poor communities that held high ideals have at times become lights that changed the world. Such was the movement of the kingdom of God that Jesus began with ordinary fishermen of Galilee. They had neither wealth nor power, but they had the ideal of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. That ideal became a source that still waters countless lives today.

Each of us, too, is a small source within society. What I cherish and what I live for affects the height of the lives of those around me. The Urantia Book regards religion as a power that elevates ideals and exalts values (see Paper 99). The Thought Adjuster who indwells us continually seeks to lift our ideals ever higher. When we respond to his leading, we not only grow as individuals but become a source that raises the stream of society. Ideals do not rise overnight. They rise little by little through the habit of meditating on truth and praying each day, and of choosing the higher way in small decisions.

Today, look honestly at how high the source of your life lies. If the heart seeks only money, convenience, and recognition, its stream will circle in low places. But if it loves truth, beauty, and goodness and longs to do the will of the Universal Father, its stream will flow clear and strong beyond me, into my family, my workplace, and the next generation.
d160.pr: Write down one ideal you want to pass on to the next generation through your life, and put it into practice once today.

msg: Paper 82 calmly describes how marriage has evolved. At its opening The Urantia Book says that marriage is man's reactional adjustment to bisexuality, while the family life is the sum total resulting from all such evolutionary and adaptative adjustments. And it declares that marriage has given mankind the home, and the home is the crowning glory of the whole long and arduous evolutionary struggle.

These words are truly astonishing. They say that the home, where a man and a woman accept each other and raise children, is a greater glory than all of humanity's achievements in gaining fire, making tools, building cities, and advancing science. The picture of primitive marriage drawn in this paper is by no means beautiful. Coercion and bargaining, property disputes and taboos were all mixed together. Yet through all that rough process humanity slowly learned love and fidelity, devotion and responsibility. The home is the fruit of that long learning. Primitive men and women united for survival rather than for love, and wives were often treated as property. But even in that harsh soil, a mother's love and a father's sense of responsibility gradually grew, until at last the ideal of marriage as a partnership of mutual respect appeared.

The passage also says that marriage is not inherent in biologic evolution, but it is the basis of all social evolution and is therefore certain of continued existence in some form. However times change and family forms diversify, the fundamental unit in which people take responsibility for one another and live together will not disappear. Paper 84 adds that the home is the true source of morality and that good parents give their children the first revelation of the love of the Paradise parents (see Paper 84). The home is not only the foundation of society but the first school of spiritual growth. Marriage and the family do not keep one fixed form forever, but their core, devotion to one another and responsibility toward the next generation, endures across the ages. As long as that core is kept, the home will always be a firm root of civilization.

Because we live so close to our homes, we easily forget their worth. The spouse and children, parents and siblings we face every day can sometimes feel like a burden. But today's passage reminds us that the home we belong to is the crowning fruit of hundreds of thousands of years of human evolution. The ordinary days of bearing with one another's shortcomings, eating together, and sharing pain are in truth a masterpiece the universe has patiently crafted over long ages. The Urantia Book also says that the family is the fundamental unit of fraternity, where patience, altruism, tolerance, and forbearance are learned (see Paper 84). One who has not learned to love family will find it hard to love all humanity as brothers and sisters.

May today be a day of seeing the home anew as a glorious gift. A warm word spoken to family, a few minutes spent truly listening, are what guard and grow this glory. If any of you carry wounds from your family, remember that the Universal Father is the true parent of all his children, and find comfort in his love. What makes a home glorious is not a fine house or ample means but the love and respect that pass between its members. A family that cherishes one another even in a poor cottage is enjoying the crowning glory of evolution.
d161.pr: Today, tell one family member in concrete words how precious they are to you.

msg: Today's passage speaks very frankly about the sex urge. It says that no human emotion or impulse, when unbridled and overindulged, can produce so much harm and sorrow as this powerful sex urge. And it says that intelligent submission of this impulse to the regulations of society is the supreme test of the actuality of any civilization. It then stresses that self-control, more and more self-control, is the ever-increasing demand of advancing mankind. These words are deeply honest, for they neither hide nor evade the problem of sex but face it squarely as a key test for measuring the maturity of a civilization.

The Urantia Book does not regard the sex urge itself as evil. It is a natural power given for the propagation of the species, and it is also the motive that gave rise to marriage and the home, humanity's highest institutions. The problem comes when that power is not governed. When a river flows within its banks, it waters the fields and nurtures life, but when it overflows its banks, it sweeps everything away. The sex urge, too, becomes a blessing when it flows within the banks of love, responsibility, and fidelity, and when those banks give way it leaves deep wounds on individuals, families, and society. Especially in an age like ours, when every kind of media constantly stirs desire, guarding these banks is all the harder and all the more precious. The words that advancing civilization demands ever more self-control foresaw exactly this reality.

The final sentence of the passage strikes us with particular sharpness today. Secrecy, insincerity, and hypocrisy may obscure sex problems, but they do not provide solutions, nor do they advance ethics. A double standard that feigns respectability outwardly while permitting license inwardly only covers the problem without solving it. The true solution lies in facing the problem honestly, governing oneself with intelligence and will, and directing that power toward a higher purpose.

Self-control is different from repression. Repression forcibly holds something down out of fear, but self-control is an act of free will that chooses a higher value. Paper 83 calls rugged self-control the acme of all human virtues (see Paper 83). The Thought Adjuster who indwells us never forces our choices, but each time we choose the higher thing, he transforms that choice into an eternal value and inscribes it in the soul. Self-control is, in the end, the path to spiritual freedom.

Self-control is not achieved by one's own strength alone. In prayer we can ask the Universal Father for strength, and the Spirit of Truth illuminates our minds, helping us discern what is true love and what is selfish desire. Sharing our hearts honestly with a trustworthy friend or community is also a great help. Just as the passage says that secrecy and hypocrisy provide no solutions, when we come into the light we more readily find the strength to overcome temptation.

Today, look not only at the sex urge but at the many other impulses that try to rule you, such as anger and greed, laziness and the like. There is no need to deny them or be ashamed of them. Simply practice building banks of love and wisdom so that they do not become your master. As small victories of restraint accumulate, we grow into freer and more beautiful personalities.
d162.pr: Name the one impulse that most often shakes you, and when it rises today, pause for a moment and catch your breath.

msg: Paper 83 shows how the institution of marriage advanced through group marriage and polygamy toward monogamy. Today's passage, like the conclusion of that progression, says that monogamy always has been, now is, and forever will be the idealistic goal of human sex evolution. It adds that this ideal of true pair marriage entails self-denial, and therefore it so often fails just because one or both of the contracting parties are deficient in that acme of all human virtues, rugged self-control. Within this short paragraph are held both the ideal of marriage and the reason that ideal collapses.

These words are an honest diagnosis of marital failure. Many people look for the reasons marriages break down in a partner's faults or differences in temperament. Such factors certainly exist. But The Urantia Book points to a more fundamental cause: true pair marriage requires self-denial, and the self-control to meet that requirement is lacking. The promise to be faithful to one person for life is a decision to lay down many other possibilities, and that decision must be kept anew every day. Feelings of love rise and fall, but the will to keep one's promise holds the relationship together even when feelings have cooled. That very will is self-control.

Paper 83 also says that monogamy is the yardstick which measures the advance of social civilization as distinguished from purely biologic evolution (see Paper 83). Animal instinct alone can never reach monogamy. It is a lofty edifice that human beings have built above instinct through reason, morality, and spiritual ideals. So monogamy is both an achievement and a task. It is not a state already attained but an ideal two people must build again together each day. Over long ages humanity arrived at monogamy through external factors such as poverty and property, but now we have reached the stage where we must keep it through the inner motives of love and fidelity.

When we hear the word self-denial, we easily feel that something is being taken from us. But self-denial within marriage is a choice made to gain something greater. When we lay down momentary satisfaction, we gain deep trust; when we bend our stubbornness, we gain a broad heart that understands the other. Couples who give of themselves little by little for each other experience an ever firmer oneness as time passes, and that oneness passes stability and peace on to their children as well.

The saying that self-control is the highest virtue does not apply to marriage alone. Self-control is the foundation of every virtue. Patience, kindness, honesty, and tolerance all come in the end from the power to govern momentary impulses and choose the better way. Jesus taught that one who rules himself is greater than one who takes a city. A life of cooperation with the Thought Adjuster means walking steadily along this very path of self-mastery.

If you are married, look today for one small thing you can gladly lay down for your spouse. If you are not, consider what self-denial is needed to keep faith in the precious relationships you have. Self-denial is not a loss but the way to a deeper love and a firmer character. One small promise kept today builds tomorrow's great trust.
d163.pr: Today, gladly set aside one of your own preferences or conveniences for the sake of someone close to you.

msg: The final part of Paper 83 deals with the ideals of marriage. Today's passage says that marriage always has been and still is man's supreme dream of temporal ideality. Though this beautiful dream is seldom realized in its entirety, it endures as a glorious ideal, ever luring progressing mankind on to greater strivings for human happiness. At the same time it advises that young men and women should be taught something of the realities of marriage, and that youthful idealization should be tempered with some degree of premarital disillusionment. It is striking that praise for the ideal and counsel about reality stand side by side within a single paragraph.

These words hold the wisdom of keeping ideal and reality together. Without ideals, marriage sinks into a mere contract for living. But ideals that ignore reality break easily and turn into disappointment. Earlier, Paper 83 pointed out that excessive romance and fantasy in courtship are one cause of the rise in divorce (see Paper 83). Those who enter marriage picturing their partner as a perfect being are bitterly disappointed when ordinary weaknesses come to light in daily life together.

The phrase premarital disillusionment may sound cold, but it is in fact a kindness meant to protect love. Married life is filled with daily meals and cleaning, money matters and child-rearing, and the clash of differing habits and temperaments. Those who know and accept these realities beforehand are not shocked when difficulties come; instead they find in them opportunities for love to mature. What remains where illusion has lifted is a deeper love that accepts the other just as they are. Love deepens not because the other is perfect but because we choose to stay together to the end even knowing their imperfection.

While cautioning against comparing marriage to the relationship between God and man, The Urantia Book says that the ideals of marriage exist on the high spheres (see Paper 83). Marriage is not a finished state but a journey on which two personalities grow together. On that journey the ideal is the star that shows the direction, and reality is the ground on which we must stand. When we gaze at the star while keeping our feet on the ground, we can move forward without falling. The gap between ideal and reality is not a sign of failure but a space for growth. As two people fill that gap together, patience and forgiveness, humility and gratitude grow.

This word is not only for young people preparing for marriage. It also gives couples who have been married for many years wisdom for dealing with the weariness and disappointment that come after the first illusions have faded. Though the first thrill may fade, the trust and friendship built by years endured together are far deeper and stronger. Cultivating eyes that recognize and treasure that deeper love is the secret of a mature marriage.

May today be a day of looking at both the ideals I hold and the reality in which I stand. If you have been disappointed in a close relationship, try accepting that disappointment as the place where illusion lifts and true love begins. The love that embraces reality without abandoning the dream is the love that lasts longest. And the love of the Universal Father, who loves each of us just as we are, is the very source and pattern of such mature love.
d164.pr: Recall one time you were disappointed in someone close to you, and pray to accept that person just as they are.

msg: Today's passage extends the relationship between men and women beyond this earthly life. Men and women need each other in their morontial and spiritual as well as in their mortal careers. The differences in viewpoint between male and female persist throughout the local and superuniverse ascensions, and even in Havona, the pilgrims who were once men and women will still be aiding each other in the Paradise ascent. Never, even in the Corps of the Finality, will these two personality trends be obliterated; always will they continue to intrigue, stimulate, encourage, and assist each other.

These words fundamentally change how we view the differences between men and women. We usually see those differences only as a source of conflict. Who can count the misunderstandings and quarrels that arise from different ways of speaking and expressing feelings, and different ways of solving problems? But in the paragraph just before, Paper 84 says that, far from giving cause for apprehension, these differences are highly beneficial to mankind. Difference is not a defect to be removed but a gift designed to complement and enrich one another.

Especially remarkable is the teaching that this difference continues into eternity. Many people think that once we enter the spiritual world, the distinction between male and female will vanish completely. Of course the reproductive function ceases after the mortal life, but The Urantia Book makes clear that the personality trends we call male and female are themselves never obliterated. The Universal Father treasures the diversity of personality and has ordained that through that diversity greater cooperation and richer experience may come about. Manliness and womanliness are a grain of personality that goes beyond bodily difference, and that grain will be refined ever more beautifully on the long journey of ascent.

Seen in this light, our present relationships with colleagues of the other sex, with spouses, and with family become the first practice ground for eternal cooperation. When husband and wife respect each other's different viewpoints and work through problems together, they are already learning the cooperation that will continue in the Paradise ascent. The same is true when men and women at work draw on each other's strengths. Rather than growing irritated that another's viewpoint differs from mine, I can be grateful that the difference widens my vision.

The passage says that men and women will be mutually dependent on cooperation in the solution of perplexing universe problems and in the overcoming of manifold cosmic difficulties. What we cannot see alone we can see together, and problems we cannot solve alone we can solve together. This principle applies not only to men and women but to all human relationships. When different beings cooperate for one purpose, that cooperation brings about far greater results than each could achieve separately. There is deep meaning in God's having made us different from one another. Whether in the family or the community, cooperation that respects difference is a rehearsal for eternal life.

Today, listen to the viewpoint of a family member or colleague of the other sex. Even if there are things you do not understand, do not judge at once; look for the wisdom hidden in that difference. That is how we begin, here and now, an eternal partnership.
d165.pr: Today, tell a family member or colleague of the other sex how their viewpoint has helped you.

msg: After treating at length the evolution of marriage and family life, Paper 84 reveals in today's passage the deepest meaning of the family. Family life is the progenitor of true morality, the ancestor of the consciousness of loyalty to duty. The enforced associations of family life stabilize personality and stimulate its growth through the compulsion of necessitous adjustment to other and diverse personalities. And even more, it declares, a good family reveals to the parents the attitude of the Creator to his children, while true parents portray to their children the first of a long series of disclosures of the love of the Paradise parent.

First, consider the words that the family is the progenitor of morality. A child first learns right and wrong at home. Sharing and yielding, promises and responsibility, admitting wrongs and asking forgiveness are first learned at home. The morality learned at school or in society mostly grows on seeds sown in the family. That is why, when the family is shaken, the moral foundation of society is shaken too. The fairness and warmth a child first experiences become the scales by which his conscience will measure for a lifetime.

The expression enforced associations is also worth noting. We can choose our friends, but not our family. Since people of differing temperaments and tastes must live under one roof, large and small adjustments are needed every day. These adjustments are sometimes hard and painful, but it is through this very process that the virtues of patience, understanding, and yielding grow. The family is like a whetstone that shapes personality; through the friction of rubbing against one another, rough edges are worn smooth. In a closeness we cannot escape, we discover our selfishness every day and learn how to rise above it.

But the climax of the passage lies in its final sentence: good parents become their children's first revelation of the love of God. When a child first imagines God, the image is borrowed from the parents. A child who has known parents who love, forgive, and are faithfully present finds it easy to believe that God is like that. Jesus called God Father precisely in order to reveal God through the relationship of love that human beings understand best.

At the same time, the passage says that parents themselves learn the Creator's heart by raising children. Through staying up nights for their children, bearing with their mistakes, and waiting for them to grow on their own, parents come to understand how the Universal Father deals with us. In loving their children, parents understand God's love more deeply, and that understanding in turn helps them love their children more wisely. This is the sacred circle that unfolds within the family. So raising children is not merely caring for a life; it becomes a spiritual discipline through which the parent's own soul grows toward the heart of God.

If you are a parent, quietly consider today what kind of God your children are meeting through you. Even those who are not parents can become someone who reflects God's love to another. Every time we love, forgive, and are patient, we are revealing, in however small a way, the love of the Paradise parent on this earth.
d166.pr: Today, consciously show a family member or someone close to you patience and forgiveness that resemble God's love.

d167.t: Awakened by the Spirit of Worship
msg: Paper 85 recounts the long history of humanity's worship of stones and hills, trees and animals, the elements of earth and sky, the sun, moon, and stars, and even human beings. Reading this list of primitive worship, one might feel it is nothing but a dark and shameful history full of superstition and fear. But today's passage tells us that an unseen hand was present throughout the whole process. Nature worship may seem to have arisen naturally and spontaneously in the minds of primitive men and women, but there was operating all this time in these same primitive minds the sixth adjutant spirit, the spirit of worship.

The adjutant spirits are the sevenfold ministry that the Mother Spirit of the local universe bestows upon the minds of evolving creatures (see Paper 36). After the spirits of intuition, understanding, courage, knowledge, and counsel, the sixth is the spirit of worship and the seventh the spirit of wisdom. This spirit was constantly stimulating the worship urge of the human species, no matter how primitive its first manifestations might be. Even in the gestures of primitive people bowing before stones and offering sacrifices to trees, there was a movement of the heart reaching toward something greater than oneself, and that movement was planted by heaven.

The passage says that the spirit of worship gave definite origin to the human impulse to worship, notwithstanding that animal fear motivated the expression of worshipfulness, and that its early practice became centered upon objects of nature. In other words, worship is not merely a by-product of fear. Fear was only the occasion; the root of the longing to worship lies in divine ministry. Human beings are made to worship. That is why no age and no people have ever lived without worship. Worship is not an invention of man but a response to a longing that heaven has inscribed in the human heart.

This truth holds important meaning for our lives today. Modern people do not worship stones or trees, but they still worship something. They put money, success, fame, pleasure, or themselves at the center of life and devote their hearts to it. The worship urge does not disappear; it only changes its object. So the question is not whether I worship, but what I worship. The spirit of worship still stirs our hearts, leading us toward the Creator rather than the creature. Examining where most of my time, money, and attention flow today is therefore a way of examining my worship.

The very next paragraph says that when the worship urge is guided by the spirit of wisdom, man begins to turn away from the objects of nature toward the God of nature (see Paper 85). When the spirit of worship and the spirit of wisdom work together, true religion begins. And since the Thought Adjuster came to indwell, that worship can deepen into living communion with the Universal Father. When we consider the long journey from the clumsy gestures of primitive people to our own quiet adoration today, we cannot help but give thanks for the patience of heaven that has guided the whole process.

Today, observe what your heart leans toward most often. Then quietly gather that heart and turn it toward the Universal Father, the source of all things. A brief word of thanksgiving, a moment of awe looking up at the sky, is a response to the long ministry of the spirit of worship.
d167.pr: Write down what your heart turns toward most often today, and offer a short prayer that places God there instead.

msg: Paper 86 shows how primitive religion grew out of the fear of chance, good luck, and bad luck. When something they could not understand happened, primitive people blamed it on spirits or ghosts. Today's passage sharply criticizes this attitude. It says that to continue to ascribe things difficult of comprehension to supernatural causes is nothing less than a lazy and convenient way of avoiding all forms of intellectual hard work. Luck is merely a term coined to cover the inexplicable, and chance is a word which signifies that man is too ignorant or too indolent to determine causes.

These words are, if anything, a deep challenge to religious people. Even among those who are said to have deep faith, many interpret every difficulty as the mischief of evil spirits or the punishment of heaven. When illness comes, they suspect a curse rather than look for a cause; when things go badly, they blame luck rather than examine their effort and wisdom. The Urantia Book says that such an attitude is not true faith but a lingering habit from primitive times. God has given us minds so that we may think, explore, and seek causes. An inquiring mind is not a sign of unbelief but the right use of a gift from the Creator.

The passage says that men regard a natural occurrence as an accident or as bad luck only when they are destitute of curiosity and imagination, when the races lack initiative and adventure. But exploration of the phenomena of life sooner or later destroys man's belief in chance, luck, and so-called accidents, substituting therefor a universe of law and order wherein all effects are preceded by definite causes. The advance of science has been exactly this process. As humanity learned that lightning is not the wrath of the gods but an electrical phenomenon, and that epidemics come not from curses but from microbes, it was greatly freed from fear.

Yet this liberation does not weaken faith. Rather, it purifies faith. A universe of law and order is not a world ruled by capricious spirits but one governed by a faithful and unchanging Creator. The Urantia Book says that the universe rests on law and order, and that these laws are the habits of God. When we explore the laws of nature, we are in fact learning the faithfulness of the Creator. Science and religion are not at war; they look at the same reality from different directions.

The last sentence of the passage is beautiful: thus is the fear of existence replaced by the joy of living. Those who live in a world whose causes they do not know are always anxious, for they never know when misfortune may strike. But those who know an orderly universe, a universe governed by a loving Father, can be at peace. Even when trouble comes, they know there is a way to understand and meet it, and they trust that God is with them through it all. Those who know this order do not lean on vague luck but live day by day in honest effort and trust.

Today, choose one thing you have attributed to luck or to someone else's fault, and honestly seek its true cause. If part of the responsibility is yours, accept it, and correct what can be corrected. When we approach life this wisely, vague fear disappears and the joy of living in God's orderly world arrives.
d168.pr: Today, choose one thing you blamed on luck or on others, and write down its real cause and what you can do about it.

msg: The last paragraph of Paper 86 seems to sum up the long history of primitive religion in a single sentence. Primitive religion prepared the soil of the human mind, by the powerful and awesome force of false fear, for the bestowal of a bona fide spiritual force of supernatural origin, the Thought Adjuster. And the divine Adjusters have ever since labored to transmute God-fear into God-love. Finally it adds that evolution may be slow, but it is unerringly effective.

These words hold a remarkable paradox. Most of the fears that tormented primitive people were false fears. The world was not teeming with evil spirits as they imagined. Even so, that fear served a purpose. Fear made human beings conscious of something greater than themselves, made them think seriously about the unseen world, and plowed the ground of the mind so that higher seed could be sown. God uses even our mistaken ideas as stepping-stones to something better. That even humanity's dark past was not in vain gives hope for our own mistakes and wanderings as well.

The seed sown in that plowed ground is the Thought Adjuster. The Thought Adjuster is a divine fragment that comes directly from the Universal Father and indwells the human mind when it makes its first moral choice (see Paper 108). The heart of the Adjuster's work is to change fear into love. Primitive people tried to appease and avoid the gods, but the Adjuster leads us to love God and draw near to him. Deep within our hearts he whispers the truth that God is not someone to fear and flee from but a Father to love and to become like.

This transformation does not happen only in the history of humanity as a whole. It happens in exactly the same way in our personal journeys of faith. Many people first approach religion because they fear punishment or dread misfortune. That is not wrong. But as faith grows, fear must gradually become trust, and trust in turn become love. If we still only fear God, the Adjuster's work has not yet borne full fruit in us. There is no fear in love, and perfect love casts out fear. One who has come to love God does his will not grudgingly but with joy.

The words that evolution is slow but unerringly effective give us patience and hope. It took hundreds of thousands of years for humanity to move from a religion of fear to a religion of love. Our personal change, too, does not happen overnight. Old anxieties and guilt, and distorted images of God, may remain. But the Adjuster never grows weary and never gives up. If only we cooperate, he will surely change the fear within us into love. Today's small trust grows into tomorrow's great love.

Today, quietly examine what fear still remains in your faith. Then hand that fear over to the Universal Father and meditate on how much he loves you. The more deeply you realize that love, the less room fear has to stand.
d169.pr: Write down one thing you still fear before God, and pray to entrust it to the Father's love.

d170.t: Good and Evil Are Not Equals
msg: Paper 87 deals with the development of the ghost cults and explains the origin of dual spiritism, the belief in good spirits and bad spirits. Today's passage says that evolutionary religion paid a terrible price for this dual concept. Early man was able to account for good and bad fortune in life only by postulating two kinds of spirits, one good and the other bad. While this belief did enable man to reconcile the vicissitudes of life with a concept of unchanging supermortal forces, it has ever since made it difficult for religionists to conceive of cosmic unity. The gods of evolutionary religion have generally been opposed by the forces of darkness.

The following paragraph reveals an even more astonishing fact. The tragedy of all this lies in the fact that, when these ideas were taking root in the primitive mind of man, there really were no bad or disharmonious spirits in all the world. Such an unfortunate situation did not develop until after the Caligastic rebellion and only persisted until Pentecost. Nevertheless, the concept of good and evil as cosmic co-ordinates is still very much alive in human philosophy, and most of the world's religions still carry this cultural birthmark.

This teaching deeply affects our view of the world. Many people imagine the universe as a battlefield where good and evil fight on equal terms. They think God and the devil contend for the human soul with roughly equal power. But The Urantia Book says this picture is wrong. The Universal Father is infinite, and there exists no source of evil equal to him. Evil arises when creatures misuse their free will; it is not another absolute principle set against God (see Paper 54). Such a dualistic picture keeps people constantly wary and anxious, and prevents them from fully trusting God's love.

The passage also tells us that the activity of evil spirits ended after Pentecost. Since Michael completed his bestowal and poured out the Spirit of Truth, evil spirits no longer enter and possess human beings (see Paper 77). Therefore, most of the temptation and evil we experience today comes from our own animal nature, our wrong choices, and the imperfections of society. Knowing this is important. If we blame every wrong on the devil, we evade our own responsibility and at the same time become gripped by needless fear.

To believe in the unity of the universe is, in the end, to believe in the sovereignty and goodness of God. There is evil and suffering in this world, but they are not eternal and can never prevail over God's good purpose. This faith gives us deep peace. However thick the darkness may seem, it is not a power equal to light; it is only a place the light has not yet reached. Rather than fearing the darkness, we need only devote ourselves to making the light shine brighter. Each time we do good, the light spreads a little further, and the darkness recedes by that much.

Today, consider whether you are fearing evil or misfortune too much, or blaming them on others. Then, trusting the one God who governs the whole universe with love, set your heart on choosing the good that lies before you.
d170.pr: When something darkens your heart today, remember the goodness of the Father who rules the universe and choose one good deed.

msg: Having surveyed the history of the ghost cults, Paper 87 looks in its final section at the value of the cult itself. The cult, that is, ritual, symbol, and forms of communal worship, has bred much superstition and waste, yet it has also served to preserve and stimulate moral sentiment and religious loyalty. Today's passage says that every new revelation of truth has given rise to a new cult, and it stresses that even the restatement of the religion of Jesus must develop a new and appropriate symbolism. This symbol must arise out of religious living, spiritual experience; it must be predicated on the concept of the Fatherhood of God and be pregnant with the mighty ideal of the brotherhood of man.

Here we are led to reconsider the relationship between form and content. Some think true faith means abandoning all forms and holding only to inner experience. But The Urantia Book acknowledges that human beings cannot live without symbols and forms. We are embodied beings, and we express and strengthen our faith through shared acts of gathering to sing, pray, and remember together. The problem is not form itself but whether the form holds living spiritual experience. Form is the vessel, and experience is the water poured into it. Without a vessel we cannot carry water, but carrying about an empty vessel means nothing.

The second paragraph points out the decisive difference between the old cults and the new. The old cults were too egocentric. Primitive cults began from the selfish motive of avoiding bad luck and gaining good luck. But the new must be the outgrowth of applied love. It must keep the functions of the old cults, fostering sentiment, satisfying emotion, and promoting loyalty, but it must do more: it must facilitate spiritual progress, enhance cosmic meanings, augment moral values, encourage social development, and stimulate a high type of personal religious living.

In light of this standard we can look again at our own worship and gatherings today. If our worship is a place where we seek only our own comfort and blessing, it still remains in the old cult. True worship draws us to God and at the same time sends us back to our neighbors. When those who have prayed together go out to help the poor, visit the lonely, and stand against injustice to establish justice, their worship becomes a new cult grown out of applied love.

The passage closes by saying that the new cult must provide supreme goals of living which are both temporal and eternal, social and spiritual. The kingdom of God that Jesus taught was exactly this. It is a spiritual reality that begins in each person's heart, and at the same time a social power that transforms relationships among people. The soul's search for God and the building of a world of brotherhood are not separate from each other. A faith that embraces both together is the healthiest faith.

Today, consider what symbols and forms the worship and faith gatherings you take part in possess, and whether they lead to applied love. When form bears fruit in the practice of love, it becomes a vessel that holds life. Do not be bound to preserving form for its own sake; look instead to the Father and the brothers and sisters to whom it points.
d171.pr: After your prayer or worship today, carry that spirit into one concrete act of love for a neighbor.

msg: Paper 88 tells in detail how fetishes, charms, and magic ruled the lives of primitive peoples. Stones and animals, hair and fingernails, names and numbers, even words became fetishes, and people believed they brought good luck or warded off bad. Today's passage gives this long history a meaningful summing up. Ancient magic was the cocoon of modern science, indispensable in its time but now no longer useful. The phantasms of ignorant superstition agitated the primitive minds of men until the concepts of science could be born. This assessment shows a balanced view that neither mocks primitive people nor glorifies superstition.

The metaphor of the cocoon is most apt. Before becoming a butterfly, the caterpillar is protected and transformed within its cocoon. The cocoon is a necessary home for that season. But if the butterfly does not shed the cocoon once it is fully grown, it cannot spread its wings. So it was with magic. Through magic, primitive people first began to think about cause and effect and tried to work with nature. Paper 88 says that the goal of science is the same as the goal of magic, and that humanity arrived at science through long experience (see Paper 88). Magic was, in effect, a clumsy first step toward science.

But the passage observes that today Urantia is in the twilight zone of this intellectual evolution. One half the world is grasping eagerly for the light of truth and the facts of scientific discovery, while the other half languishes in the arms of ancient superstition and but thinly disguised magic. These words fit today's reality exactly. Even people who use the most advanced technology still reckon lucky and unlucky days, carry charms, and give their hearts to fortune-telling and horoscopes. Only the outward appearance is modern; deep in the heart, the cocoon of magic still remains.

This warning matters for religious people too, because magical thinking often carries on in the name of faith. Believing that prayer is answered only if certain words are repeated exactly, regarding some object as containing God's blessing, or fearing punishment for omitting a ritual are all remnants of magic. The true religion The Urantia Book teaches is personal communion with God and doing his will. God is not a power to be manipulated with spells or charms but a Father to be loved and trusted.

To shed the cocoon of magic means to hold scientific spirit and spiritual faith together. It means exploring facts honestly, seeking causes wisely, and on that foundation trusting God. Such faith is free, not bound by fear. It does not strive to buy good luck or lean on superstition to escape bad luck. Instead it walks with God each day and faithfully carries out the work entrusted to it. This is the soul become a butterfly, spreading its wings.

Today, look for any magical thinking that still lingers in your thoughts and habits. If you find even one small superstition, lay it down and put simple trust in the Universal Father in its place. Free of superstition, we enjoy the liberty to fly in a wider sky and explore the truth.
d172.pr: Find one superstition or fortune-telling habit you follow without thinking, and from today offer a prayer of thanks in its place.
